item.title: 12 tips for people who posted on LinkedIn but now wanna post on X A lot of people I know are moving their posting from LinkedIn to X. When they ask me how I grew 80k followers on X in one year, here’s what I tell them: 1. LinkedIn is a stage. X is a party. First you find your crowd, then you liste...
item.description:
作者：Zara Zhang 账号：@zarazhangrui 简介：Builder. Harvard’17. Instagram: https://t.co/aJqTEMrL2L YouTube: https://t.co/8xzbGWtf6w GitHub: https://t.co/KCuEajezlL
12 tips for people who posted on LinkedIn but now wanna post on X
A lot of people I know are moving their posting from LinkedIn to X. When they ask me how I grew 80k followers on X in one year, here’s what I tell them:
1. LinkedIn is a stage. X is a party. First you find your crowd, then you listen to what they're already talking about. Don't start talking until you get it
2. You can't reach the C-suite directly. LinkedIn is a professional network, so you can go straight to decision makers. X doesn't work like that. You have to get mass attention first, and then the right people notice you
3. Post way more than you think. On LinkedIn, 3-5 posts a week counts as a lot. I posted 3 times a day on X for 6 months. Some founders I follow post 5 times a day. It's not that they're on X all day. They just don't overthink it
4. Make posting a reflex. If you spend too long on a post, you won't post. Whenever a thought comes up, post it right there. No planning, no scheduling, no waiting for the right time
5. It's a numbers game. Most posts won't do well. Maybe 1 in 10 will. Maybe 1 in 50 goes viral. That's normal
6. Half your posts should be reactions. LinkedIn is mostly “proactive content”. On X, at least at the start, half of what you post should be “reactive content”: replies, quote tweets, commentary on what others already said
7. Know the difference between a reply and a quote tweet. A reply is like a LinkedIn DM. It says "notice me." A quote tweet uses someone else's content to grow your own account
8. Fix your feed first. If you wanna talk about cybersecurity and your feed is all politics, you can't join the right conversations. Pick a few big names in your niche. See who they follow and who they engage with, and follow those people too. Like, bookmark and comment. After about a week your timeline will look totally different
9. Write like you're texting an acquaintance. Polish turns people off. Everyone's allergic to perfect AI-sounding writing. And please don't use AI or bots to write your replies. People can tell, and they might block you
10. Post the stuff that's obvious to you. Make a list of the top 10 questions customers, investors and your team ask you. That's where you're the expert. What seems too obvious to talk about is exactly what people want to hear
11. Post what you just said out loud. If you say something in real life and people go "huh, never thought of it that way," post it on your way back. Don't wait, you'll forget. You don't have to block out time to think of what to say. Just say what you've already said
12. Show your face, and don't sell yet. X is a wall of text, so video stands out. I just record myself on my laptop with something on the screen. People wanna know you're a real human, not AI slop. And until you have about 1,000 followers, don't promote your company. Share real opinions first. Later, when you repost company news, always add your own take, not PR speak.
Remember: people follow people, not companies

item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Huge opportunity right now to build new services firms from the ground up, or transform existing ones, with agents at the center.
The expertise that services firms in theory should have is as important as ever because you still need deep domain understanding to get the most out of agents. But now the ability to deliver on projects has a 10X multiplier. This means that you can make clients happier, compete to win more of them, go after smaller customers not in the TAM before, or deliver outcomes that weren’t really conceivable.
This is going to happen in advertising, IT transformation, management consulting, finance, and a number of other fields that historically are just fully constrained by the speed of their workforce for output.
This is a huge opportunity right now for those starting these firms. I wouldn’t count out existing players that commit to the transformation either as existing customer trust goes a long way. But they have to move quickly to make it work.

item.title: The Revolution vs The Renaissance — Thariq Shihipar, OpenAI
item.description:
播客：Latent Space
And I, um, don't even really feel like I'm bottlenecked by intelligence maybe. Like, maybe I'm bottlenecked by ambition. Like, maybe if I had like a, a larger thing. AI is both, uh,
like a industrial revolution and a renaissance, you know? Do we want the model to truly improve itself completely headlessly? It's like not clear to me that, um, this will even be the best option.
[upbeat music] Hello, we're back again with a series of episodes we recorded at the recent AIE Code Summit, and we're releasing them all in the next week or so.
And today we're bringing back one of your favorite guests, Tariq Schipkar, uh, most recently of Anthropic, but as of today he's announced that he's joining OpenAI.
And we go a little bit into his thinking and what is fascinating him about building with agents.
He gave the closing keynote at AIE Code, and it was very well received, and I really like the overall framing of the, it revolution versus the renaissance.
One of the top buzzwords of this entire year is the software factory, and actually, uh, interestingly, a lot of the messaging around AIE was that we maybe rushed too quickly to the factory.
Uh, and even if we do have the factory, it frees us up to do the other side of the productivity gains, which is the renaissance.
So we have the revolution that has made software cheaper, more reliable, easier to produce at scale, and also produces a lot of slop.
But also the renaissance makes it affordable to build something personal, to raise the level of your art, to spend time and human in the loop refining how it feels.
So both revolution and renaissance can happen in the same project, and that's what he talks about in the, in the talk, and we go a little bit deeper in the podcast as well.
And really, his message is that you wanna get the feedback loop back. You- we spend a lot of time taking the human out of the loop for agents, uh, to be autonomous, to be dark factories and all those things.
But really, uh, he thinks that to have more s- taste, you want to actually put some of that human feedback loop in to actually make it easy to build ephemeral tools to just try stuff out.
And once you try stuff out, you will know because the human has actually tried it. And I think a lot of slop is produced because the human is not really dogfooding and testing enough.
So he has a slash human skill, uh, that he shows. And it also comes from a lot of intuition from building things that are s- technically perfect, right?
Like the, the, the model thinks they've done a perfect job, it's a perfectly balanced game, it's a good macOS dock app, but then you don't use it. And why don't you use it?
It's because you never used it during building it. And that comes from a lot of introspection, and I think it's also a little bit behind his thinking on what he's planning to do next.
When he announced moving to OpenAI, both Thibault and Andrew said that basically it is time to reinvent Codex. So it's kind of open-ended what he means.
There's a few slides in there that I think betray a little bit of thinking. I'm speaking for myself, not for him. But I think it's overall a super interesting conversation, and I'm glad to share it with you today.
